pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: Data and AI projects fail in predictable places: the data was not what anyone thought, nobody agreed what good looks like, or the client cannot run the thing after you leave. This workspace is built around those three risks.
The four tables
Engagements

: one row per piece of client work. Stages follow how this work really runs: Discovery, Proposal sent, Data audit, Pilot, a Go or no-go decision, Production, then Handed over. Each shows fee type, contract value, whether data access is granted and whether personal data is in scope, plus hours, cost and delivery margin rolled up from time entries.
Clients
: industry, data maturity and the executive sponsor, with engagements won and contracted value.
Deliverables
: audit reports, gap maps, dashboards, models, evaluation sets, runbooks and training. Each has Accepted when written in the client's words and, for models and assistants, an Evaluation score.
Time entries
: hours by consultant at their cost per hour, unbilled, invoiced or non-billable.
A normal week
Monday: the managing partner reads Live engagements and the Waiting on the client list. Anything in review over five days gets a call to the sponsor.
Each consultant logs time daily from the engagement with Log time.
Every model or assistant deliverable has its evaluation run before Client review, with the score recorded.
At the Go or no-go stage the sponsor decides with the pilot numbers in front of them; write the decision in the engagement page.
Friday: unbilled time is checked against fee type and invoiced.

When Personal data in scope is ticked, data stays in the client's environment, access is named per person, and the handover includes how to remove our access.

pages.title: From discovery to a go or no-go

text.text: Most failed AI projects were never set up to succeed: the question was vague, the data was thinner than promised, or nobody said what result would be good enough. This page is the path every engagement takes before real money is spent.
Discovery (one to two weeks)
Write the business question in one sentence the sponsor agrees with, for example "Cut stock-outs in the top 200 products by a third."
Name the number that will move and how it is measured today.
List the systems, tables and documents involved, who owns them, and whether personal data is in them.
Data audit (two to three weeks)

cells.text: Missing values, missing months, missing stores
How late the data arrives after the event
A named person who can explain each table
Whether the data can answer the business question at all

text.text: The audit ends with a gap map: each gap, its effect on the question, and what fixing it costs. Sometimes the right answer is to stop here and fix the data first.
Pilot (four to eight weeks, fixed fee)
One use case, on real data, with the people who will use it.
Agree Accepted when before building: for a model, the error on held-out data; for an assistant, the share of an agreed question set answered correctly with a source.
Build the evaluation set with the client's experts, not from our own guesses.
Report the score honestly, including the cases it gets wrong.
The go or no-go meeting
Score against the agreed bar
Cost to run in production, per month
Who on the client side will own it
What it would take to reach the bar if it fell short
A no-go is a good outcome when the evidence says so. Write it down and close the engagement cleanly.
A model or assistant is only finished when the client's team can check it and run it without us. This page covers how we evaluate before review and what a complete handover contains.
Evaluation before every client review
Run the agreed evaluation set on the exact version being delivered.
Record the score in Evaluation score on the deliverable.
Read every failure, not just the total. Group them: missing source document, wrong number, out-of-date policy, misunderstood question.
Fix the biggest group first and re-run. Never tune on the evaluation set itself; keep a held-back slice nobody looks at until the end.
Move the deliverable to Client review only when the score meets Accepted when.
What we tell the client

cells.text: 87 of 100 policy questions answered correctly with a citation
Questions about plans retired before last year
Monthly hosting and usage at current volume
The evaluation set and the command or button that runs it

text.text: Handover checklist
Runbook: how to run, monitor, re-train or update the documents
Evaluation set and how to re-run it
Dashboards or alerts for drift and errors
Training session with the people who will own it
Our access removed, listed person by person
Sponsor sign-off, then press Mark handed over
After handover

Offer a short advisory retainer for the first months. The usual questions are about drift: the business changed, the data changed, and the score quietly fell. A monthly re-run of the evaluation set catches it early.
Worked example

The service desk assistant pilot scored 78 percent against an 85 percent bar. Grouping failures showed most came from three outdated policy pages; once the client replaced them, the score rose to 84 and the next round targets the remaining phrasing gaps.
